Forgiven Ways BEE Easy

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
According to former employees, self styled prophet Ernest van Antwerpen is using his Forgiven Ways Group to circumvent BBBEE legislation and pocket the earnings for himself and his ministry.

Unique Selling Point:
Ernest van Antwerpen is a self proclaimed prophet and messenger of God. His teachings fall under what he calls a Yahushua-Culture and are in themselves quite controversial, amongst others he has published "Prayers against homosexual sins" and claims the African continent is poor because "Africa is poor due to the idolatry and the occult behaviour of African people." But Ernest has also created an extremely complex company structure under a trust called the Forgiven Ways Group. And he is using the trust and specifically one of the entities under the group called BEE-Easy in a BEE fronting scam that rakes in millions and does very little in the sense of actual Black Economic Empowerment.

Summary:
BEE-Easy targets South African corporates through existing BEE legislation which allows for benefits such as increased BEE ratings and tax exemptions. For example, a corporate can sponsor a BEE candidate for a learnership for 1 year. IT will cost the corporate between R30 000 - R40 000 per learner, and a monthly stipend for the learner of between R1500 - R3000 p/m. The corporate pays the amount, in many cases upfront, to BEE Easy to facilitate the process. But according to former employees and learners, the money is channeled by Ernest to his church and pastors. In 2018 BEE Easy took in 400 learnerships. But students say that from day one they were treated badly. At the BEE Easy offices they had one toilet to share between all the students, with no refreshments offered during the day. They did not receive monthly stipends on time or at all. And some of them have now not received the certificates promised despite completing the courses. Former BEE Easy staff members were forced to attend monday morning prayer sessions at the offices. Ernest's teaching in Yahushua-culture was offensive to many of them. In June 2017 BEE-Easy stopped paying their salaries, and if they complained they were told they were going against God. Many left after three months of no payment and BEE EAsy still owes them the money. But they have simply hired new staff, taken in new corporate customers, and carried on with the business. While doing so, they have offered many existing NGO's the opportunity to become fully black owned by partnering with Forgiven Ways, which is supposedly black owned. But they have hijacked the existing NGO's and NPO's projects, under the promises of huge growth potentials and capital investments that never happened. So Forgiven Ways ends up with controlling shareholding in the projects, but runs them into the ground and don't pay what they promised.

Further information:
We have many case studies to back up the claims, including people whose projects have been stolen, learners and former staff.

There is a possibility that we will receive financial documents that will prove that Forgiven Ways misappropriated the funds they took in for learnerships.

A lawyer, who is handling cases for the former employees and people's whose companies and projects have been hijacked, and who has won at least one court action against Ernest is willing to give us an on-camera interview. He has sent us a brief description of what he is willing to say and I have forwarded the mail to Anna-Maria.

Press Release:


BEE Easy
South Africa relies on the effective implementation of black economic empowerment (BEE) policies to bring – especially – the youth into the economic mainstream through learnerships and business partnerships. But often, BEE is undermined by ruthless companies, clamouring for corporate sponsorships for their BEE initiatives. Carte Blanche investigates how a not-for-profit company raked in millions of Rands, while allegedly doing very little real empowerment for its beneficiaries.
Producer: Graham Coetzer
Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender


Script:


Forgiven Ways
2nd Draft 6 March 2019


Voice
What do hundreds of thousands of rands in missing stipends, a drug rehab project gone wrong, and a slew of irate ex-employees have in common? They’re all linked to this man, self proclaimed prophet Ernest van Antver/pin.

Sound Up Cheryl Dorreson
I had been introduced to Ernest and Susan through another lady, who heard about my change management program, and she said that’s awesome I have a company that I’ll refer you to, and I’m sure that they will be able to use your services as a change consultant.

Voice
Early last year Cheryl Dorreson, and fellow change management consultant Mpati Khuele, were employed by Ernest and his business partner Susan van Aswegen. Their jobs involved mentoring about 300 young people who were studying a Generic Management Learnership at one of Ernest and Susan’s many businesses, Haggai Education and Training. Mpati says she had misgivings from day one.

Sound Up Mpati
Joining an NPC, which is supposed to be a holding company with subsidiaries that are businesses for me was, you know, a bit uncomfortable.

Voice
Ernest and Susan have put together a complex business structure called the Forgiven Ways Group, aimed at providing large corporates with Broad Based Black Economic Empowerment solutions. At the top of the pyramid is the Forgiven Ways non profit company or NPC, in which Ernest is a director. It’s a faith based organisation where Ernest spreads his often controversial version of God’s word to poor communities.Then comes companies for profit like BEE-Easy, which offers to help optimise your BEE Levels and Haggai Education and Training which offers skills development. Below those are at least another 55 companies in industries such as construction, transport, retail and mining. All of the entities claim to be between 51% and 100% black owned.

Voice
Cheryl and Mpati say they first noticed something was wrong when they didn’t get paid their salaries last year.

Sound Up Cheryl
It was on the day that we were supposed to get paid, we got a phone call, saying that there’s been a problem and we wouldn’t get paid today, and it would get rectified.

Voice
But one month soon turned into three without salaries, and despite their passion for the work they were doing, they were eventually forced to quit. And they weren’t the only people not being paid. Haggai Education and Training makes its money by offering learnerships to young BEE candidates in need. The learnerships are paid for by large corporates who can improve their BEE scorecard and get tax deductions for sponsoring the students. By Susan’s own admission they had 300 learners last year and got paid on average R40 000 per student, a total of roughly R12 million. On top of that corporates also pay Haggai a monthly stipend of a few thousand rand each which is to be paid directly to the learners. Karabo Kolai from Orange Farm jumped at the chance to complete a learnership last year, but says Haggai failed to deliver on some of the promised stipends.

Sound Up Karabo Kolai
They would tell us that the companies that are paying our stipends are being bankrupt, sometimes they don’t say anything they will tell us that the person that is paying our stipend is not around.

Voice
Karabo says she and her fellow students were heavily dependant on the money.

Sound Up Karabo
Like we’re not only calculating the transport money, we’re even calculating the food allowance. I must have food. Like even if I bring lunch from home, I must buy bread, to make lunch, to take to school.

Voice
Last week, we met with Ernest and Susan at their offices in Meyersdal. We wanted to know where the black owners of companies like Forgiven Ways and Haggai were.

Sound Up Ernest and Susan
Devi: Haggai is 51% black owned, is it?

Susan: IT’s owned by Forgiven Ways non profit ultimately.

Devi: So Forgiven Ways non profit has a 51% share in…

Susan: Haggai

Devi: In Haggai. Where’s the black ownership here?

Susan: So, a non profit’s shareholder, really is the beneficiaries. So the beneficiaries that get benefitted in the non profit, that is where the black comes from.

Devi: As the beneficiaries?

Susan: Yes and that’s according to the BEE codes.

Devi: Yes.

Susan: A non profit is allowed to take up shareholdership in a company, and it derives its black from its beneficiary status.

Voice
This may well comply with BEE legislation, but Mpati would have liked to see more black owners.

Sound Up Mpati
For me, you know, I would have loved to see beneficiaries empowered into and trained into ownership of the company. You know you can’t own a company and you are like a virtual owner of a company, you’re not hands on, no one is mentoring you, coaching you, in how the company can be run.

Voice
But Ernest and Susan don’t seem too keen on the idea of having actual black shareholders.

Sound Up Ernest and Susan
Devi: Why don’t you have black shareholders, I mean real black shareholders, not beneficiaries.

Susan: Then we have fat cats, and our mission is that we need to benefit the masses.

Devi: But you guys are shareholders?

Ernest: 51% is Forgiven Ways, and that money goes to, to…
Devi: No, wait wait, are you guys shareholders or not shareholders?

Susan: Sorry, the other shareholder is Alt In, of which 50% of that is actually our staff. And the other 50%…

Devi: And you guys? a, so you’re a fat cat as well now? If you don’t want to give black people shareholding?


Susan: Its minimal, the shareholding that’s in there.

Voice
They admitted to owing employees salaries dating back to last year.

Sound Up Ernest and Susan
Devi: So this outstanding salary bill is about R800 000, that’s owed?

Susan: Yes

Devi: Thats a lot of money?

Susan: Yes, but not an impossible amount for where we stand right now.

Voice
Yet, they took in new learners for this year, while still owing stipends to last year’s group.

Sound Up Ernest and Susan
Devi: And how much would you say you’re still owing for students? How much do you think? Is it a lot of money? Is it half that amount?

Susan: Less than a million.

Devi: Less than a million.

Voice
And they had a surprising reason for not having paid.

Sound Up Ernest and Susan
Susan: We had an event, where some funds were taken from our account from SARS side, because we were in the process of putting our payment arrangement in place. Unfortunately that was some of our stipend funds.

Devi: But how can you be operating like this where you’re in a situation where you have not paid SARS, you have not paid salaries, then SARS takes the money out of your account, now these… I mean you keep saying you’re going to walk the path, I mean what path do you want these learners to walk with you if you’re not even paying money thats due to them.

Susan: You know what, I think for learners even it is a choice. If you do want to develop.

DEvi: No, its not a choice.

Susan: It is…

Devi: No, no, no. You chose to run this as a business. Gos spoke to him, you guys got this together, you chose to do this. Those learners, the money was already paid into your bank accounts. And they were already paid, that’s just not right.
Susan: I think the point is…

Devi: No, no, the point is that’s just not right.

Susan: I didn’t say it’s right.

Devi: You shouldn’t have been put in a situation where you can’t pay people you owe.

Susan: IT wasn’t our doing.

Devi: Now you’re blaming who now, SARS?

Susan: No

Devi: Who, you’re blaming who?

Susan: I’m just saying its something that happened, it was not supposed to have happened, it happened. We are here to sort it out.

Voice
Russel Florence is also an ex-employee who is still owed money on his salary. He sees himself as a BEE activist and says initially he was thrilled to join the Forgiven Ways Group.

Sound Up Russel
Devi: Were you excited at the prospect?

Russel: Yes I was. I looked at the work that BEE Easy and Forgiven ways wants to do for township economies.

Voice
Last year Russel identified a project that Ernest and Forgiven Ways promised to sponsor. A group of about 40 drug addicts were moved from the mean streets of Eldorado Park to a farm in Mpumalanga to undergo rehabilitation and counselling. But Forgiven Ways soon stopped paying, and Russel was stuck trying to raise the funds to at least provide the men with three square meals a day. Eventually the project ground to a halt.

Sound Up Russel
Half of those guys have relapsed. I get phone calls everyday from parents that says please help our children.

Sound Up Ernest
Devi: So what happened to the project?

Ernest: We are not stopping that project, we are going forward with that project, when we receive funds again for that project. But things happen, and we need to step in faith. We don’t want that to happen to people, we love them. But we are stepping in faith and the turn around is around the corner.

Link Devi
Ernest says he receives visions from the Lord, and even if they are controversial, it’s his job to put the message out there.

Voice
Cheryl and Mpati say they were expected to attend weekly teachings where Ernest explained the visions he received, some of which are set out in this book Ernest wrote and distributed to staff.

Sound Up Cheryl & Mpati
Devi: Tell me about the monday morning meetings?

Cheryl: They made me very angry. It was just totally… It was like getting a tongue lashing from the principal.

Devi: Were they compulsory?

Cheryl: Yes

Voice
Ernest denies that the monday morning meetings were compulsory, and says he can’t help it that people find his teachings offensive.

Sound Up Ernest and Susan
Devi: Then there’s the other piece under the heading prayer against homosexual sins.

Ernest: Yes

Devi: Lets go through that. God gave you a vision of a tsunami hitting Cape Town and i quote, you say: “You homos of Cape Town, the rest of South Africa and beyond, stop sinning now. Step away from your disgraceful acts of lusty animal behaviour.” God said this to you?

Ernest: Yes. That’s not good words, and I, one thing that God told me, who am I to change God’s words. I cannot change God’s word.

Devi: I’m listening to what you are saying, and whatever you’re saying I’m taking with respect, but I find this highly offensive.

Ernest: Ja, I have to tell people what God is telling this country. But he wants us to tell the truth so that they can change.

Devi: Your truth?

Ernest: I believe that I’m telling you God’s truth.

Devi: Which is a different truth from somebody else’s?

Ernest: That’s fine.

Link Devi
Take away irate staff members, business deals gone wrong and a complex company structure, you’re left with students who believed that their futures held brighter promises.

Voice
Two days after our interview with Ernest and Susan, Russel, Cheryl, Mpati and 15 other former employees received a first instalment of the monies owed to them. But Mpati says her biggest disappointment is how Forgiven Ways let learners like Karabo down.

Sound Up Mpati
You give them hope, you employ a whole team to mentor them, to get them ready for employment, and in that process you break them even further.






Forgiven Ways PROMOS
PROMO 1
Voice
Despite raking in millions through his complex Broad Based Black Economic Empowerment businesses, a self proclaimed profit stands accused of failing to deliver on his promises to staff and students.


PROMO 2
Voice
We investigate a non profit company and the self proclaimed prophet who heads up the organisation, and find a tale of unpaid stipends, irate staff and goodwill projects gone seriously wrong.

PROMO 3
Voice
Unpaid SARS bills, a fear of so-called fat cats and a slew of allegations against a self proclaimed prophet and his business partner. What went wrong at non profit company Forgiven Ways?

It’s a faith based organisation where Ernest spreads his often controversial version of God’s word to poor communities.Then comes companies for profit like BEE-Easy, which offers to help optimise your BEE Levels and Haggai Education and Training which offers skills development. Below those are at least another 55 companies in industries such as construction, transport, retail and mining. All of the entities claim to be between 51% and 100% black owned. Voice Cheryl and Mpati say they first noticed something was wrong when they didn’t get paid their salaries last year. Sound Up Cheryl It was on the day that we were supposed to get paid, we got a phone call, saying that there’s been a problem and we wouldn’t get paid today, and it would get rectified. Voice But one month soon turned into three without salaries, and despite their passion for the work they were doing, they were eventually forced to quit. And they weren’t the only people not being paid. Haggai Education and Training makes its money by offering learnerships to young BEE candidates in need. The learnerships are paid for by large corporates who can improve their BEE scorecard and get tax deductions for sponsoring the students. By Susan’s own admission they had 300 learners last year and got paid on average R40 000 per student, a total of roughly R12 million. On top of that corporates also pay Haggai a monthly stipend of a few thousand rand each which is to be paid directly to the learners. Karabo Kolai from Orange Farm jumped at the chance to complete a learnership last year, but says Haggai failed to deliver on some of the promised stipends. Sound Up Karabo Kolai They would tell us that the companies that are paying our stipends are being bankrupt, sometimes they don’t say anything they will tell us that the person that is paying our stipend is not around. Voice Karabo says she and her fellow students were heavily dependant on the money. Sound Up Karabo Like we’re not only calculating the transport money, we’re even calculating the food allowance. I must have food. Like even if I bring lunch from home, I must buy bread, to make lunch, to take to school. Voice Last week, we met with Ernest and Susan at their offices in Meyersdal. We wanted to know where the black owners of companies like Forgiven Ways and Haggai were. Sound Up Ernest and Susan Devi: Haggai is 51% black owned, is it? Susan: IT’s owned by Forgiven Ways non profit ultimately. Devi: So Forgiven Ways non profit has a 51% share in… Susan: Haggai Devi: In Haggai. Where’s the black ownership here? Susan: So, a non profit’s shareholder, really is the beneficiaries. So the beneficiaries that get benefitted in the non profit, that is where the black comes from. Devi: As the beneficiaries? Susan: Yes and that’s according to the BEE codes. Devi: Yes. Susan: A non profit is allowed to take up shareholdership in a company, and it derives its black from its beneficiary status. Voice This may well comply with BEE legislation, but Mpati would have liked to see more black owners. Sound Up Mpati For me, you know, I would have loved to see beneficiaries empowered into and trained into ownership of the company. You know you can’t own a company and you are like a virtual owner of a company, you’re not hands on, no one is mentoring you, coaching you, in how the company can be run. Voice But Ernest and Susan don’t seem too keen on the idea of having actual black shareholders. Sound Up Ernest and Susan Devi: Why don’t you have black shareholders, I mean real black shareholders, not beneficiaries. Susan: Then we have fat cats, and our mission is that we need to benefit the masses. Devi: But you guys are shareholders? Ernest: 51% is Forgiven Ways, and that money goes to, to… Devi: No, wait wait, are you guys shareholders or not shareholders? Susan: Sorry, the other shareholder is Alt In, of which 50% of that is actually our staff. And the other 50%… Devi: And you guys? a, so you’re a fat cat as well now? If you don’t want to give black people shareholding? Susan: Its minimal, the shareholding that’s in there. Voice They admitted to owing employees salaries dating back to last year. Sound Up Ernest and Susan Devi: So this outstanding salary bill is about R800 000, that’s owed? Susan: Yes Devi: Thats a lot of money? Susan: Yes, but not an impossible amount for where we stand right now. Voice Yet, they took in new learners for this year, while still owing stipends to last year’s group. Sound Up Ernest and Susan Devi: And how much would you say you’re still owing for students? How much do you think? Is it a lot of money? Is it half that amount? Susan: Less than a million. Devi: Less than a million. Voice And they had a surprising reason for not having paid. Sound Up Ernest and Susan Susan: We had an event, where some funds were taken from our account from SARS side, because we were in the process of putting our payment arrangement in place. Unfortunately that was some of our stipend funds. Devi: But how can you be operating like this where you’re in a situation where you have not paid SARS, you have not paid salaries, then SARS takes the money out of your account, now these… I mean you keep saying you’re going to walk the path, I mean what path do you want these learners to walk with you if you’re not even paying money thats due to them. Susan: You know what, I think for learners even it is a choice. If you do want to develop. DEvi: No, its not a choice. Susan: It is… Devi: No, no, no. You chose to run this as a business. Gos spoke to him, you guys got this together, you chose to do this. Those learners, the money was already paid into your bank accounts. And they were already paid, that’s just not right. Susan: I think the point is… Devi: No, no, the point is that’s just not right. Susan: I didn’t say it’s right. Devi: You shouldn’t have been put in a situation where you can’t pay people you owe. Susan: IT wasn’t our doing. Devi: Now you’re blaming who now, SARS? Susan: No Devi: Who, you’re blaming who? Susan: I’m just saying its something that happened, it was not supposed to have happened, it happened. We are here to sort it out. Voice Russel Florence is also an ex-employee who is still owed money on his salary. He sees himself as a BEE activist and says initially he was thrilled to join the Forgiven Ways Group. Sound Up Russel Devi: Were you excited at the prospect? Russel: Yes I was. I looked at the work that BEE Easy and Forgiven ways wants to do for township economies. Voice Last year Russel identified a project that Ernest and Forgiven Ways promised to sponsor. A group of about 40 drug addicts were moved from the mean streets of Eldorado Park to a farm in Mpumalanga to undergo rehabilitation and counselling. But Forgiven Ways soon stopped paying, and Russel was stuck trying to raise the funds to at least provide the men with three square meals a day. Eventually the project ground to a halt. Sound Up Russel Half of those guys have relapsed. I get phone calls everyday from parents that says please help our children. Sound Up Ernest Devi: So what happened to the project? Ernest: We are not stopping that project, we are going forward with that project, when we receive funds again for that project. But things happen, and we need to step in faith. We don’t want that to happen to people, we love them. But we are stepping in faith and the turn around is around the corner. Link Devi Ernest says he receives visions from the Lord, and even if they are controversial, it’s his job to put the message out there. Voice Cheryl and Mpati say they were expected to attend weekly teachings where Ernest explained the visions he received, some of which are set out in this book Ernest wrote and distributed to staff. Sound Up Cheryl & Mpati Devi: Tell me about the monday morning meetings? Cheryl: They made me very angry. It was just totally… It was like getting a tongue lashing from the principal. Devi: Were they compulsory? Cheryl: Yes Voice Ernest denies that the monday morning meetings were compulsory, and says he can’t help it that people find his teachings offensive. Sound Up Ernest and Susan Devi: Then there’s the other piece under the heading prayer against homosexual sins. Ernest: Yes Devi: Lets go through that. God gave you a vision of a tsunami hitting Cape Town and i quote, you say: “You homos of Cape Town, the rest of South Africa and beyond, stop sinning now. Step away from your disgraceful acts of lusty animal behaviour.” God said this to you? Ernest: Yes. That’s not good words, and I, one thing that God told me, who am I to change God’s words. I cannot change God’s word. Devi: I’m listening to what you are saying, and whatever you’re saying I’m taking with respect, but I find this highly offensive. Ernest: Ja, I have to tell people what God is telling this country. But he wants us to tell the truth so that they can change. Devi: Your truth? Ernest: I believe that I’m telling you God’s truth. Devi: Which is a different truth from somebody else’s? Ernest: That’s fine. Link Devi Take away irate staff members, business deals gone wrong and a complex company structure, you’re left with students who believed that their futures held brighter promises. Voice Two days after our interview with Ernest and Susan, Russel, Cheryl, Mpati and 15 other former employees received a first instalment of the monies owed to them. But Mpati says her biggest disappointment is how Forgiven Ways let learners like Karabo down. Sound Up Mpati You give them hope, you employ a whole team to mentor them, to get them ready for employment, and in that process you break them even further. Forgiven Ways PROMOS PROMO 1 Voice Despite raking in millions through his complex Broad Based Black Economic Empowerment businesses, a self proclaimed profit stands accused of failing to deliver on his promises to staff and students. PROMO 2 Voice We investigate a non profit company and the self proclaimed prophet who heads up the organisation, and find a tale of unpaid stipends, irate staff and goodwill projects gone seriously wrong. PROMO 3 Voice Unpaid SARS bills, a fear of so-called fat cats and a slew of allegations against a self proclaimed prophet and his business partner. What went wrong at non profit company Forgiven Ways?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): According to former employees, self styled prophet Ernest van Antwerpen is using his Forgiven Ways Group to circumvent BBBEE legislation and pocket the earnings for himself and his ministry.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Ernest van Antwerpen is a self proclaimed prophet and messenger of God. His teachings fall under what he calls a Yahushua-Culture and are in themselves quite controversial, amongst others he has published "Prayers against homosexual sins" and claims the African continent is poor because "Africa is poor due to the idolatry and the occult behaviour of African people." But Ernest has also created an extremely complex company structure under a trust called the Forgiven Ways Group. And he is using the trust and specifically one of the entities under the group called BEE-Easy in a BEE fronting scam that rakes in millions and does very little in the sense of actual Black Economic Empowerment.
metadata.Summary: BEE-Easy targets South African corporates through existing BEE legislation which allows for benefits such as increased BEE ratings and tax exemptions. For example, a corporate can sponsor a BEE candidate for a learnership for 1 year. IT will cost the corporate between R30 000 - R40 000 per learner, and a monthly stipend for the learner of between R1500 - R3000 p/m. The corporate pays the amount, in many cases upfront, to BEE Easy to facilitate the process. But according to former employees and learners, the money is channeled by Ernest to his church and pastors. In 2018 BEE Easy took in 400 learnerships. But students say that from day one they were treated badly. At the BEE Easy offices they had one toilet to share between all the students, with no refreshments offered during the day. They did not receive monthly stipends on time or at all. And some of them have now not received the certificates promised despite completing the courses. Former BEE Easy staff members were forced to attend monday morning prayer sessions at the offices. Ernest's teaching in Yahushua-culture was offensive to many of them. In June 2017 BEE-Easy stopped paying their salaries, and if they complained they were told they were going against God. Many left after three months of no payment and BEE EAsy still owes them the money. But they have simply hired new staff, taken in new corporate customers, and carried on with the business. While doing so, they have offered many existing NGO's the opportunity to become fully black owned by partnering with Forgiven Ways, which is supposedly black owned. But they have hijacked the existing NGO's and NPO's projects, under the promises of huge growth potentials and capital investments that never happened. So Forgiven Ways ends up with controlling shareholding in the projects, but runs them into the ground and don't pay what they promised.
metadata.Further information: We have many case studies to back up the claims, including people whose projects have been stolen, learners and former staff. There is a possibility that we will receive financial documents that will prove that Forgiven Ways misappropriated the funds they took in for learnerships. A lawyer, who is handling cases for the former employees and people's whose companies and projects have been hijacked, and who has won at least one court action against Ernest is willing to give us an on-camera interview. He has sent us a brief description of what he is willing to say and I have forwarded the mail to Anna-Maria.
